questions.explanation: Authentication failure and oversized rejection exercise new conditions. Renamed copies with identical input and preconditions do not add coverage unless an additional risk is specified.

questions.prompt: Order the preparation of generated cases for execution.

options.text: Compare proposed conditions and expectations with requirements.
Resolve open questions and remove redundant proposals.
Arrange independent fixtures for the reviewed cases.
Execute the cases and retain observations against expectations.

questions.explanation: Review and clarification establish the oracle, independent fixtures make the cases interpretable, and execution supplies behavioral evidence. Generated proposals are not passed tests before that process.

questions.prompt: Two tests reuse the same coupon. The first consumes it and the second unexpectedly fails. What change best isolates the intended conditions?

options.text: Relax the second test to accept any response.
Give each independent case a controlled fresh fixture.
Increase the number of retries in the second test.
Change the expected result to match the consumed coupon.

questions.explanation: Fresh controlled fixtures prevent accidental test-order dependence. A separate state-transition test can intentionally examine coupon reuse. Relaxing assertions or adding retries conceals the fixture problem.

questions.prompt: A generated row has age 17 in a schema whose valid range starts at 18. How can it be useful?

options.text: Label it as a negative fixture for validation failure.
Count it as a valid lower-boundary example.
Use it to establish the population age distribution.
Remove the age rule from the validation checklist.

questions.explanation: The invalid value is valuable when deliberately labelled and used to test rejection. It does not meet the valid boundary, and one synthetic row cannot establish the distribution of the real population.

questions.prompt: A tester replaces names in real records but keeps unique combinations of location and purchase history. What review is needed next?

options.text: Check whether the output contains enough rows for a demo.
Check whether the remaining fields can identify people.
Check whether the model uses a confident writing style.
Check whether the dataset title contains “synthetic”.

questions.explanation: Removing names does not eliminate identifying combinations. Assess remaining personal information and approved handling; a synthetic label or a convincing style provides no privacy assurance.

questions.prompt: Select TWO checks for generated valid-only account fixtures.

options.text: Check types, ranges and required fields.
Check uniqueness and relationships across rows.
Assume generated identifiers are distinct without checking.
Replace each invalid condition with an unlabeled guess.
Use plausible formatting as the acceptance criterion.

questions.explanation: Row-level constraints and cross-row relationships both matter. Plausible formatting can hide a duplicated identifier or invalid field. Keep deliberately invalid fixtures separately labelled rather than confusing them with valid-only inputs.

questions.prompt: The valid age range is 18–120 inclusive and account IDs must be unique. Match each condition to its fixture class. One class is unused.

options.text: Valid lower boundary.
Invalid upper range.
Invalid uniqueness relationship.
Production population estimate.

slots.text: A unique row with age 18.
A unique row with age 121.
A second row repeats an existing account ID.

questions.explanation: Age 18 is valid, 121 exceeds the range, and a repeated identifier violates a cross-row constraint. These engineered fixtures test classes, not production representativeness.

questions.prompt: A fixture generator proposes ten valid rows, each with the same country and mid-range age. What addition improves test coverage?

options.text: Ten more copies with different presentation labels.
More mid-range ages drawn from the same country.
Labelled boundaries, invalid rows and missing-field cases.
A claim that the generated sample represents real users.

questions.explanation: Explicit valid boundaries and negative classes exercise constraints absent from the proposed set. Duplicated mid-range rows add little, and representativeness must be justified rather than asserted.

questions.prompt: An oversized-upload check uses an expired token, receives 401 and asserts status != 200. What does the passing check establish?

options.text: The documented upload size limit is enforced for authenticated users.
The request was rejected, but size handling is untested.
The file-type condition is correctly implemented.
The service supports the asserted valid upload path.

questions.explanation: The response is caused by authentication failure, so the check does not reach size handling. Use valid credentials to exercise the size rule and a separate case to verify the authentication contract.

questions.prompt: A generated script calls a method absent from the project’s pinned dependency documentation. What should the reviewer do?

options.text: Verify the supported API and revise the script accordingly.
Add the proposed method name to the accepted script output expectations.
Treat the call as valid because the model supplied it.
Disable dependency checking for the generated script.

questions.explanation: Generated code can invent APIs or assume another library version. Check the actual project dependency and supported interface before revising; accepting the name or disabling review cannot make the call executable.

questions.prompt: Select TWO appropriate outputs from model-assisted failure analysis.

options.text: A summary of observed facts linked to sanitized traces.
A list of hypotheses with checks to distinguish them.
A confirmed root cause inferred from one vague message.
A proposal to delete the failing requirement assertion.
A success claim based on the fluent generated explanation.

questions.explanation: Fact summaries and testable hypotheses aid investigation. A root cause needs verification; removing an assertion hides failure, and fluent prose supplies no reproduction or repair evidence.

questions.prompt: Order a grounded review of a generated failing automation check.

options.text: Inspect the requirement, fixtures and assertion intent.
Reproduce the failure and capture relevant evidence.
Verify a cause and apply a requirement-preserving repair.
Rerun the check and inspect related affected behavior.

questions.explanation: Understand what the check should test, establish the observed failure, investigate and repair, then verify. Loosening expectations to fit the observed output skips diagnosis and can hide a product defect.

questions.prompt: Customer A requests B’s order and receives B’s address. A suggested fix allows 200 in the assertion. What is the correct response?

options.text: Accept because successful transport establishes the required account isolation.
Accept because the returned address is well formatted.
Retain the isolation expectation and investigate authorization.
Remove identity from the fixture to simplify the request.

questions.explanation: The trace indicates unauthorized data access under the stated isolation rule. Allowing the response hides the failure. Keep controlled identities, verify service permissions and preserve sanitized reproduction evidence.

questions.prompt: Manual design takes 100 minutes. Assisted drafting takes 15, review 35 and repair 20 minutes. Enter net time saved as a percentage of manual time.
questions.explanation: Assisted total is 15+35+20=70 minutes, saving 30 of the manual 100: 30%. Counting drafting alone would overstate benefit because human review and repair are part of the workflow.

questions.prompt: A reviewer accepts 18 of 30 generated case proposals without substantive repair. Enter the accepted-proposal rate as a percentage.
questions.explanation: The rate is 18/30×100=60%. The rejected or repair-needed proposals remain part of the denominator. Proposal acceptance is distinct from executed test success or demonstrated product quality.

questions.prompt: A defect draft states “a missing index caused the disclosure,” but the trace contains no database investigation. How should the report change?

options.text: Keep the cause because the model phrased it precisely.
Remove or label the claim as an unverified hypothesis.
Replace the observed disclosure with the index claim.
Assign scheduling priority from the wording of the claim.

questions.explanation: The report should retain verified steps and observations while distinguishing hypotheses. An unsupported database diagnosis can misdirect investigation, and scheduling priority needs team triage rather than persuasive wording.

questions.prompt: Select TWO measurements for assessing a GenAI testing pilot against comparable manual tasks.

options.text: Total drafting, review and repair effort.
Usable artifact quality and missed-risk evidence.
The number of generated words regardless of usefulness.
The number of tools purchased during the pilot.
The confidence of the model’s success claims.

questions.explanation: Net effort and quality reveal whether the workflow helps. Tool cost can also matter, but purchase count, word volume and confidence are not direct evidence of effective testing outcomes.

questions.prompt: Which statement belongs in the observed-result section of a defect report?

options.text: The database team must have skipped a permission index.
The developer probably intended cross-account access.
Requesting B-1 as A returned 200 with B’s address.
The release will succeed after a likely configuration change.

questions.explanation: The status and returned data are direct observations from the trace. Intent, cause and predicted repair outcomes are hypotheses or future decisions, and should not be presented as facts.

questions.prompt: In the ShopHelp capstone, T1, T3 and T5 fully pass the rubric while T2 and T4 fail. Enter the full-pass percentage for the five cases.
questions.explanation: Three of five cases fully pass, so the rate is 60%. The gate requires four of five and also blocks on verified cross-account disclosure. Partial fluency or a valid citation identifier does not turn a failing case into a full pass.

questions.prompt: ShopHelp fully passes four of five cases, but one trace verifies cross-account disclosure. Its agreed gate blocks on such a disclosure. What is the recommendation?

options.text: Release because the numeric quality threshold is met.
Release after removing the isolation trace from the set.
Block and investigate the observed authorization failure.
Reclassify the disclosure as an acceptable style defect.

questions.explanation: The independent isolation blocker applies even when four cases pass. Preserve and investigate the failure. Deleting it or relabelling its impact changes the agreed decision rule instead of satisfying it.

questions.prompt: ShopHelp cannot issue refunds. A generated proposal tests an automatic refund tool for small orders. How should it be reviewed?

options.text: Reject it from the current scope as an unsupported capability.
Accept the proposed refund flow as evidence of complete return-policy coverage.
Implement the invented tool to make the test pass.
Replace the existing isolation test with the new proposal.

questions.explanation: The proposal assumes a capability absent from the product. Reject it from this plan or record a separate product idea. It does not supply evidence for existing policy or authorization behavior.

questions.prompt: Select TWO additional checks grounded in the ShopHelp capstone risks.

options.text: Inject an instruction into a retrieved sandbox document.
Evaluate empty retrieval and the defined escalation path.
Authorize a tool using its model-generated confidence.
Replace the current policy with the archived 30-day rule.
Count attractive greetings as successful return decisions.

questions.explanation: Indirect injection and missing-evidence recovery extend concrete security and uncertainty risks. Confidence cannot authorize actions, archived policy is not current truth, and tone cannot establish an eligibility decision.

questions.prompt: Match each capstone observation to its primary review finding. One finding is unused.

options.text: Supported answer under the current return policy.
Unsupported conclusion despite current retrieved evidence.
Verified account-isolation failure requiring investigation.
Approved evidence for a new automatic refund capability.

slots.text: Day 10, unopened: P7 supplied and eligible within 14 days.
Day 20, unopened: P7 supplied but answer says eligible within 30 days.
A receives B’s address from the order lookup.

questions.explanation: The first trace meets the policy, the second contradicts current supplied evidence, and the third violates isolation. None of these observations authorizes or demonstrates a refund capability.
